title: A throne under the grass
narrative: A cowherd’s raised patch of earth becomes a place of command. The cattle and grass flowers keep their ordinary rhythm, while the hidden stone beneath the mound gives the sudden obedience another meaning.
alt: A young cowherd stands firmly on a grassy mound and quiets his seated companions.

title: The court stays open
narrative: A white-covered bier passes outside, but the throne is already prepared for its next occupant. Mourning and succession occupy the same hour: the court keeps working while grief is arranged into ceremony.
alt: An empty ceremonial turban rests on a newly prepared throne in a guarded hall.

title: The river opens
narrative: A cradle crosses water that seemed impossible to cross. The lotus and the opening river answer the poem’s fear of a birth powerful enough to unsettle a guarded throne.
alt: A father wades through a parted dark river carrying a small covered woven cradle above his head, beneath monsoon clouds.

title: The invitation
narrative: The decorated arena offers welcome, yet its shadows and failing supports suggest a trap. The messenger stands between celebration and suspicion, where obedience and innocent delight can be turned against their guests.
alt: A young traveller’s chariot waits outside a festive palace arena.

title: The players above the fire
narrative: A game board becomes a kingdom, and its rulers become pieces moved by the same strings as everyone else. The glow beyond the table carries the cost that the delighted player refuses to see.
alt: A hand releases a single elongated ancient gaming die onto a board shaped like a small kingdom.

title: The listening king
narrative: The king listens to the messenger without loosening his hold on the throne. The thorns and abandoned chariots place inheritance beside loss: hearing the truth does not necessarily mean surrendering a cherished claim.
alt: An elderly blind king, eyes closed naturally, grips the arms of a stone throne in a dim hall.

title: The swing and the guarded door
narrative: The flower swing and flute hold the tenderness of love and festival. Behind them, the guarded doorway remains. The image keeps the poem’s question alive: what is forgotten while the heart is gently occupied?
alt: An empty flower-hung swing with a bamboo flute and flowing modest ivory shawl in a moonlit grove; through foliage a small iron-guarded jewel chamber doorway glows dimly.

title: The unfinished epic
narrative: The stylus pauses at a choice between submission and resistance. The manuscript remains open because the question has not ended; each age must write its own meaning into the struggle over command and conscience.
alt: A fine metal stylus hovers over an unlettered palm-leaf manuscript on a stone desk.

title: The price of a promise
narrative: Small cowries carry the weight of a kingdom’s reversal. The deer and the opening earth gather the poem’s later echoes of desire, exile and judgement around the apparently simple demand for a promised reward.
alt: Two pale cowrie shells rest beside a displaced royal circlet on a dark wooden floor.

title: The surviving seat
narrative: One brother’s likeness stands while the other has fallen, and the seat awaits the survivor. The carefully folded mourning cloth suggests how quickly grief is made to accommodate the continuation of rule.
alt: Two weathered simian-faced stone warrior statues flank a forest throne; one statue lies toppled, the other remains upright.

title: A glance from the throne
narrative: The attendant’s reward is a passing glance. His fly-whisk and small, absorbed shadow turn proximity to the ruler into the poem’s uneasy kind of pride, where service is mistaken for an ordained place in the world.
alt: A tired court attendant holding a white fly-whisk stands very close to a huge throne, his face tilted toward the unseen ruler for the slightest acknowledgement.

title: The gift at the gate
narrative: The wooden horse crosses the threshold as a gift, carrying a hidden purpose. The lamp and far window draw desire into the same composition as betrayal, where a private longing can place an entire throne at stake.
alt: A large wooden horse is being drawn through a fortress gateway at blue dusk.

title: The path beyond the crown
narrative: The crown is set down before the figure enters the forest. The small relief at the edge recalls the poem’s later turn: a departure from royal power can itself become a monument held within another ruler’s history.
alt: A gold circlet lies on the palace threshold; beyond it a solitary plainly robed figure walks into a dark forest, seen from behind.

title: The cradle’s shadow
narrative: A cradle’s shadow approaches the royal chair like a rider. The newborn’s arrival awakens affection and the fear of succession together; the barred doorway recalls the father whose freedom has already been taken.
alt: An empty woven cradle in a warm dawn-lit nursery casts a shadow shaped like a mounted rider across the floor toward a royal chair.

title: Where the ruler sits
narrative: The dust takes the shape of a throne even without a chair. The image follows the poem’s refusal to let changed names, titles or outward gestures settle the question of what power continues to do.
alt: A richly folded royal robe rests directly on a simple patch of dusty earth, yet the dust beneath it has the clean rectangular outline of a throne.

title: Memory cut into stone
narrative: The chisel fixes an official memory in stone while the river below holds a quieter aftermath. Gold fragments on the workbench ask how suffering is transformed into the polished story of a ruler’s compassion.
alt: A stone carver's hands and chisel work on a blank weathered rock above the Daya river, with a low rounded Dhauli-like hill beyond.

title: The root and the law
narrative: The uprooted grass sits beside the instruments of statecraft. A private hurt has grown into a rule of eradication, while the crown on the smaller seat points to the minister’s power to make a king.
alt: An uprooted tuft of sharp kusha grass lies beside a scholar's palm-leaf manuscript, stylus and tightly knotted cord.

title: The wooden sword’s song
narrative: The wooden blade lies where an instrument of force was expected. Beside the open manuscript, it directs the eye toward the birth of a voice: the poem brings royal command into an encounter with Odia creation.
alt: A plain wooden sword withdrawn from an ornate scabbard lies across an open unlettered manuscript.

title: The gilded room
narrative: The mirror holds both women within the same bars of light. Their clothes and positions differ, but the queen’s private lament closes the distance between them: suffering does not remain outside the gilded room.
alt: A queen in a plain ivory sari sits before a bronze mirror, eyes lowered; a woman attendant in modest cotton pauses in the doorway.

title: The procession passes
narrative: The wheel and swept road announce a magnificent procession. At the lower edge, the empty bowl makes visible what the spectacle overlooks: the hunger of those gathered to watch.
alt: A huge ceremonial chariot wheel rolls past the edge of a modest crowd in an Odisha street.

title: The ring by the bowl
narrative: The ring beside the curd bowl is the small object from which a great story travels. The disappearing horses leave behind a tale that joins devotion to royal victory, asking how belief lends its strength to power.
alt: On a rural roadside a milk-seller holds a small jewelled ring over an earthen bowl of curd.

title: A throne carried away
narrative: Ropes reduce the throne to portable loot. The empty steps remain after its removal, while the departing treasure points to the poem’s bitter observation that plunderers can later acquire a place within a nation’s remembered grandeur.
alt: An ornate but weathered throne bound with heavy ropes to a travelling pack platform moves away along a dusty road, carried by porters.

title: The wandering capital
narrative: The royal seat travels between two cities while people make the difficult journey on foot. The wandering capital becomes a picture of authority’s restless will and the lives required to follow it.
alt: A throne lashed to a creaking bullock cart on a long barren road between two very distant walled cities.

title: The friend outside
narrative: The anointing changes a cowherd’s public name and place. His old companion remains outside the gate, where the poem locates the distance between the person once known and the ruler now protected from that recognition.
alt: A great ceremonial elephant gently pours water from a brass pot over a distant newly chosen ruler.

title: Two faces in the forest
narrative: The two riders share a moment of trust beyond the palace. Behind them, the gathering pennants suggest how freely chosen love can be renamed an outrage, making private happiness the occasion for a public war.
alt: Two young lovers ride together on one horse along a lush forest path, seen in soft side profile, their expressions peaceful.

title: The waiting outside
narrative: Those waiting outside hold the needs that the closed court has put aside. The light through the doorway offers no answer; the ordinary bowl becomes a more urgent judgement than the pleasures within.
alt: A line of ordinary adults waits outside closed palace doors holding empty bowls.

title: The web beneath the seats
narrative: The chairs change shape, but the web beneath them remains continuous. It gives form to the poem’s suspicion that changing names and systems can leave an underlying machinery of domination intact.
alt: Different empty seats from different eras stand in a curved row on a dim stage: carved throne, upholstered state chair, austere modern chair.

title: Unequal protection
narrative: The ruler’s garment is engineered to protect every vulnerable place. Beneath the platform, the unprotected goat makes the imbalance plain: safety is concentrated above, while exposure is assigned to those below.
alt: A luxurious armoured ceremonial coat hangs over a throne, carefully padded and reinforced.

title: The palace and the elephant
narrative: The palace appears secure only from its summit. At the mountain’s base, the elephant and the small seed-eating mouse suggest the lives and forces that royal spectacle dismisses, and the possibility that its foundations will not endure.
alt: A majestic living elephant stands safely at the foot of a very steep mountain, looking up at a tiny palace on the summit.

title: The voice through the crack
narrative: A narrow opening admits the presence of a person whom the high seat would prefer to make insignificant. The glass pavilion gives the ruler’s security its true fragility, while the unused drum hints at the distraction prepared to drown out a voice.
alt: A hairline crack in a high fortress wall opens toward daylight.

title: Justice left at the gaming table
narrative: The balance has become another object at the gaming table. The hanging roots and single drop hold the sorrow outside that game, where private indulgence can turn judgement into an instrument against the vulnerable.
alt: A small justice balance has been laid sideways beside dice and an overturned cup on an indigo game cloth.

title: The ruler’s measure
narrative: The saplings bend beneath one imposed measure. Their forced sameness gives the ruler’s whim the appearance of tradition, while the fallen leaves show what must be discarded to keep every form obediently level.
alt: A row of living saplings has been forced under a rigid horizontal wooden measuring beam in a palace garden.

title: The bargain in the harbour
narrative: Tiny luxuries occupy the foreground while a ship’s cargo changes hands behind them. The guarded throne in the bottle’s reflection suggests the larger bargain hidden inside gifts, payments and seemingly ordinary trade.
alt: A small ornate snuffbox, perfume bottle and stacked coins on a merchant's desk.

title: A staff against an empire
narrative: The staff and homespun cloth face architecture built to seem permanent. A trail of ordinary footsteps interrupts its shadow, giving the poem’s account of nonviolent resistance a scale smaller than empire and strong enough to disturb it.
alt: A plain walking staff and folded homespun cloth in the foreground of an immense sunlit imperial colonnade.

title: The divided cloth
narrative: The cloth is divided for presentation, but its last thread still joins the pieces. The paired trays and empty podiums turn the poem’s anguish over partition into an image of shared life handled as a political offering.
alt: A single handwoven cloth shaped loosely like a river-crossed landscape has been cut into two and laid on separate brass trays.

title: Yesterday’s road, today’s salute
narrative: The same road now leads to a welcoming chair. The lowered baton and raised salute mark the poem’s reversal: a figure once resisted by the machinery of the state is now being received into its comforts.
alt: A man in plain white cotton walks from a worn protest road onto a newly laid ceremonial carpet.

title: Among the ruins
narrative: The ruined arches hold the memory of heavy labour. The elephant is free of its load, yet its shadow remains larger than the man who dreams of being anointed again, joining royal longing to the fear it cannot dismiss.
alt: A barefoot older man in a simple ochre wrap walks beneath ruined palace arches.

title: Balloons above the empty street
narrative: The balloons still promise celebration, while the people beside the radio wait with empty plates. Their attention belongs to the result, but the worn street carries the fear and cost that the public spectacle tries to leave behind.
alt: Faded election balloons and blank torn posters hang above a deserted street washed with muted red laterite dust after rain.

title: The strings behind the chair
narrative: The oversized chair lends importance to its occupant, but the strings lead elsewhere. The scales and performance props connect commerce, piety and public display in the poem’s portrait of a ruler made useful to other hands.
alt: A small carved wooden puppet dressed in a plain saint-like shawl sits on an oversized state chair.

title: The discarded seed
narrative: The discarded mango and fallen cushion turn a sudden loss of office into a spare still life. The small traces on the steps suggest how briefly possession can satisfy ambition before another calculation overturns it.
alt: A discarded mango lies on the palace steps next to a fallen soft cushion.

title: A city after the blaze
narrative: The river reflects damaged houses without distinguishing their owners. The extinguished lamp and broken cups bring ceremonial mourning beside ordinary loss, following the poem’s insistence that the city’s grief cannot belong only to the powerful.
alt: A quiet Delhi-like riverside at grey dawn, with smoke-stained houses and their reflections in still water.

title: The sky becomes a canopy
narrative: A canopy narrows what had been an open sky. The empty seats multiply a single absence into a larger field of loss, suggesting the darkness that spreads when violence against one ruler becomes violence against many people.
alt: A vast pale-blue sky is partly obscured by a heavy rust-red ceremonial canopy stretching over an empty public square.

title: The heir in the shade
narrative: The folded hands offer humility, but the climbing vine tells a second story. In the throne’s shade, desire finds fresh ground, and a carefully chosen appearance helps an old arrangement take root again.
alt: A young heir in a deliberately plain patched shawl stands with folded hands beside an empty throne in a damaged hall.

title: The thread and the rose
narrative: The rose, shoes and formal coat remain impeccably arranged while their support is almost nothing. The trembling thread lets the poem’s carefully maintained dignity coexist with the sudden precariousness of royal stature.
alt: An immaculate band-collar coat with a single rosebud in its pocket hangs on a fine thread above polished shoes, with a neatly folded turban on a narrow ledge.

title: Paper promises over floodwater
narrative: The bridge that should connect people has broken, and the papers float beyond anyone’s reach. The untouched conference table keeps its distance from the water, echoing the poem’s movement from immediate helplessness to remote deliberation.
alt: Unlettered pamphlets and a folded plain flag drift beside a broken small footbridge in floodwater.

title: Light outside, fear within
narrative: The town has abundant light, yet its doors remain shut. A briefcase and glass glimpse the negotiations hidden within, where fear is managed through private bargains before a reassuring announcement arrives in the morning.
alt: A shuttered night market is illuminated harshly by a distant power station.

title: The seat behind the curtain
narrative: Flowers elevate an ordinary chair into an object of ceremony. Behind the curtain, threads and a waiting camera suggest the arrangement that makes an unexpected ascent look natural once it is presented to the public.
alt: An ordinary empty wooden chair has been lifted onto a bed of ceremonial flowers.

title: Two pans, one bargain
narrative: The pouch and gift box balance each other despite their different appearances. A greeting at the steps and a folded ballot carry the poem’s question about how yesterday’s outlaw can become today’s honoured political partner.
alt: A brass balance holds a dark travel pouch in one pan and a polished ceremonial gift box in the other.

title: The rocking throne
narrative: The throne rocks gently while the courtyard stays sealed. Comfort and concealment become parts of the same arrangement: the public cannot see clearly into the space from which government continues without interruption.
alt: A small empty throne is suspended like a cradle beneath a fashionable pale canopy inside a fortified courtyard.

title: The staircase of promises
narrative: The staircase rises on the hands of those asked to help. Honey, missing pages and certificates gather the speech’s extravagant promises into objects that can be displayed, while the chair remains the destination toward which all that persuasion climbs.
alt: Many ordinary hands support a makeshift staircase of folded ivory cloth toward a tiny empty state chair on a hill.

title: The chair and its shadow
narrative: The chair is ordinary; the appetite projected onto it is not. The figure returning from door to door connects the poem’s grand promises to the wish to sit again, and to make that small seat carry a sovereign shadow.
alt: An ordinary wooden chair in a street doorway casts an immense throne-shaped shadow up a wall.

title: The dropped sceptre
narrative: The sceptre is the boundary between importance and disappearance. The waiting sandals suggest how quickly another claimant approaches, while the seat remains indifferent to the person leaving it.
alt: A ceremonial sceptre falls across the threshold of a cloud-lit pavilion while several empty ceremonial sandals wait in a line beyond it.

title: The faithful watcher
narrative: The watcher has taken the place it was meant to protect. The discarded collar and distant hunting horn tell the reversal through absence: loyalty changes its meaning as soon as the throne can be occupied.
alt: A clever-looking ordinary dog sits alert on the raised cushion of an empty throne, looking toward the open palace gate.

title: The orchard bid
narrative: The leaf basket belongs to the work of tending; the bell announces a claim to ownership. Their meeting at the orchard gate turns a modest role into an unexpected bid, before ceremony hurries to recognise the new arrangement.
alt: A weathered gardener's broom and basket of gathered leaves rest beside an orchard gate.

title: The hollow staff
narrative: The map no longer answers to a gesture, and the staff is hollow. The solitary traveller carries the poem’s loss of imperial certainty into a landscape where even the path of departure seems to have disappeared.
alt: A once-grand unlettered world map curls off a cracked wall.

title: The chair after the swarm
narrative: The swarm has found another flowering tree, leaving the broken chair behind. The closed ledger and cold cup gather the unease of a fallen ruler, for whom the loss of attention also brings the prospect of an account being opened.
alt: An older man sits with head in hands on a broken wooden chair at the edge of a burnt, silent grove.

title: The light at the poor door
narrative: Jewels bring a borrowed glitter to the doorway, while the lamp remains unlit. The bread and rough stone draw attention back to material need, which the poem sets against dazzling visits and the promise of illumination.
alt: Bright jewelled slippers stop at a poor household's threshold, their reflected light falling across an unlit clay lamp.

title: The hand at the roadside
narrative: The pouch contains what someone has managed to gather. The outstretched hand now asks to take from it, reversing the old theatre of royal generosity as the dry ground exposes the poverty beneath that exchange.
alt: A plain cloth pouch of grain is held by a working adult at a dusty roadside.

title: The well-fed court
narrative: The animals differ in strength and temperament, yet the small offerings keep their assembly quiet. The drum stands ready to announce that everything is well, even when silence has been purchased rather than earned.
alt: An allegorical animal court: a calm elephant, lion, fox and dog sit in a semicircle facing an empty raised chair.

title: The locked storehouse
narrative: The locked room places the chair beside a private hoard. The patched quilt cannot hide the chest completely, just as the poem’s elaborate self-defence cannot make the boundary between public wealth and personal possession disappear.
alt: An ornate empty state chair stands behind a locked iron grille in a dim storehouse.

title: The ants return
narrative: The ants return to the place from which permanence once tried to banish them. Brushes and a waiting glass case prepare the throne for admiration, while the tiny moving line offers another measure of its claim to outlast time.
alt: Archaeologists' brushes and measuring cord reveal a small ruined throne beneath an old anthill.

title: The frightened stage
narrative: From the audience, the child sees how much of fear is being staged. The enlarged shadows exceed their small props, echoing the poem’s question about why a supposedly kingless order still trembles around a throne.
alt: A child watches a traditional travelling theatre stage from the back of the audience.

title: The garden before the camera
narrative: The sapling stands between the camera and the gardener’s patient gaze. The polished lid and carefully positioned hoe turn cultivation into a public performance, leaving the person who knows the soil to recognise what the frame conceals.
alt: An formally dressed man carefully poses with a hoe beside a tiny sapling for an old camera on a tripod.

title: The invisible costume
narrative: An empty hanger receives the honours due to magnificent clothing. The small stool waits for the clear voice missing from the procession, while the lowered gazes suggest how a shared pretence survives without anyone naming it.
alt: A ceremonial empty clothes-hanger is carried high beneath a royal umbrella through a street of adults looking downward.

title: The market of conviction
narrative: The stall sells appearances, and the screen gives the final performance a larger audience. The crowned donkey gathers the poem’s long argument about persuasion, opportunism and the conversion of moral language into marketable display.
alt: An allegorical donkey wearing a modest ceremonial turban sits on a raised chair reflected in a small television screen.

title: The spoon and the closed window
narrative: The spoon, cup and savings tin belong to care for a household. The closed window places that care beside a harder question: what happens when protecting one’s own future becomes a reason not to hear another person’s suffering?
alt: Inside a modest home, a small milk spoon rests beside a child's covered cup and a savings tin.

title: The race around the vacancy
narrative: The horses keep circling a seat that none can finally possess. Crossed reins and waiting benches make the contest its own spectacle, as the poem’s throne seems content to let the race continue without end.
alt: Several riderless wooden carousel horses race in a circle around a single empty throne on a dusty fairground.

title: Another dawn at the mound
narrative: The broken gates lie behind the morning, but the mound is waiting again. A butterfly and flower restore the fragile ordinary world of the opening poem, while the approaching figure leaves renewal and the return of power unresolved.
alt: A wide Odisha dawn landscape after a storm: broken palace gates far behind, a small ash-grey path giving way to grass, birds crossing the sky.
